title: Mira's groom
hookLine: a little princess is told Krishna is her groom and never forgets; ishta devata, and why people have 'their' mantra
carry: one face of god becomes your ishta
tomorrow: tied to a stone and thrown into the sea, a saint sang five syllables
last: ABHYASA IS PRACTICE THAT WORKS IN THE DARK.

cards: A little girl in a royal family in Rajasthan watches a wedding procession go past: drums, horses, a groom glittering on his way. She tugs her mother's sleeve. Who's going to be my groom?
Her mother, maybe half joking, points to the small image of Krishna in the house. Him. Giridhar Gopal.
The little girl believes her, completely. And she never stops.

teach.h: MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL, NO ONE ELSE.
teach.b: That girl is Mirabai, the singer you met back on day sixteen. Historians know only a little about her life for sure; this is the story as it's told, and sung.
She grew up, was married into a royal family, and kept singing to Krishna anyway. Her best-known line is simple: mere to Giridhar Gopal, dusro na koi. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, no one else.
Hinduism has a word for what Mira had.
Ishta: desired, cherished, chosen. You met it on day six, in ishta devata, your chosen form of God.

Many Hindus speak of one divine reality with many faces: Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna, Rama, the Goddess, Ganesha. The ishta is the face a person is drawn to, and many say it finds you as much as you find it.
Choosing one face isn't calling the others wrong: one truth, many names, as day six put it. And a person's mantra usually belongs to their ishta.
How does it come? In many lineages a guru gives it in a ceremony called diksha, initiation, and it's kept private. Some families have a family deity, and the mantra comes with the family.
And some people, like Mira, are simply drawn, and keep returning. All three are real paths. This week you'll meet four mantras sung openly: for Shiva, for Ganesha, for Krishna, and the Gayatri.
You're not being asked to pick a god.

teach.h: ONE FACE OF GOD BECOMES YOUR ISHTA.
teach.b: You're noticing which sound your heart keeps going back to.

how: Many Hindus have an ishta devata, a chosen form of God, and a personal mantra tied to it; in many lineages the mantra is given privately by a guru at initiation (diksha), while others inherit a family deity's mantra or are drawn to one over time. Mirabai's songs to Krishna are still sung in homes and temples.

o: the one you cherish and choose

games.q: match the story to the teaching.

s: every Hindu picks their own mantra by trying a few
in many lineages a guru gives it at diksha; some inherit a family deity's; some find it by being drawn.
the one you love and choose, as in ishta devata.
choosing an ishta means rejecting the other gods
one truth, many names: Mira's Krishna was hers without anyone else being wrong.

games.q: your friend's family prays mostly to Shiva, but she keeps feeling drawn to Krishna. what fits today's teaching?
o: many Hindus would say that pull may be her ishta showing itself; she can honor it without dropping her family's Shiva.
she has to stick with the family god, or it doesn't count.
she should stop praying until she's sure which god is strongest.
games.why: an ishta can be given, inherited or found, like Mira's. choosing one face doesn't make the others wrong.

practice: After a few slow breaths from your routine, say softly or silently, on the out-breath, Om three times, then Ram, the name of Rama, three times, then Shanti, peace, three times, noticing how each one sits.
You don't have to believe anything to try them; just listen for which one your body wants to say a fourth time. Then say that one, slowly, for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Ishta. Chosen, cherished. The face of God a person is drawn to, and the mantra that comes with it.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: one face of God becomes your ishta. Mira's was Giridhar Gopal. That is day one hundred four.
